name: Hund's Rule
statement: Fill each empty orbital of a shell singly, with parallel spins, before pairing any up.
meaning: Within a set of orbitals of equal energy, electrons spread out — one to each orbital, all spinning the same way — before any orbital takes a second electron. Put formally, of the arrangements available to a configuration, the one with the greatest number of unpaired parallel spins, the highest total spin, sits lowest in energy. It is the rule that tells you how electrons distribute themselves across a degenerate subshell, and so fixes an atom's ground state.
mechanism: The familiar single rule of maximum multiplicity is really the first of three that together fix an atom's ground-state term under the standard coupling scheme: first maximise the total spin, then, among those, maximise the total orbital angular momentum, and finally settle the fine-structure level — lowest for a subshell half-filled or less, highest for one more than half-filled. The stabilisation of parallel spins traces to the Pauli principle, which keeps same-spin electrons apart. The textbook story that they therefore repel one another less is, taken literally, wrong: careful calculation shows the deeper cause is reduced screening of the nucleus, which pulls the electrons inward and increases their attraction to it.

examples.text: Carbon's two 2p electrons go into separate orbitals with parallel spins rather than pairing in one, giving a spin-one ground state — the plainest illustration of the rule.
Nitrogen's three 2p electrons each take their own orbital, all spins aligned, giving three unpaired electrons and an unusually stable half-filled subshell.
The rule leaves molecular oxygen with two unpaired electrons in a triplet ground state, which is why liquid oxygen is drawn to a magnet — a direct, visible consequence.

variants.name: The three rules in full
variants.text: The complete prescription: maximum total spin, then maximum orbital angular momentum, then the fine-structure level set by whether the subshell is at most or more than half filled — the second and third rules resolving what the first leaves open.

variants.name: Exchange stabilisation
variants.text: The quantum bookkeeping behind the rule — the energy lowering that comes from the antisymmetry the Pauli principle demands of same-spin electrons, the exchange or Fermi hole.

whyItMatters: It is one of the working rules by which chemists and physicists read off the ground state of an atom or ion, and it underlies the magnetic character of matter: whether a substance has unpaired electrons, and so whether it is paramagnetic, follows directly from how its degenerate orbitals fill. From the colours of transition-metal complexes to the reactivity of molecular oxygen, the pattern the rule describes runs through chemistry.

working.text: when filling orbitals of equal energy, place one electron in each with the same spin before doubling any up.
to judge whether an atom or ion is paramagnetic, use the rule to find how many unpaired electrons its ground state carries.
apply the rule to find the lowest state of a configuration, not to rank the excited ones above it, where it is unreliable.

limits: The rules are empirical, drawn from atomic spectra, and reliable chiefly for the ground state of light and medium atoms; they should not be trusted to order the excited states of a configuration. They assume the coupling scheme in which electron repulsion dominates spin-orbit interaction, which holds for lighter elements but breaks down in heavy atoms, where strong spin-orbit coupling makes a different scheme appropriate and the third rule in particular can fail. Genuine exceptions exist even among molecules. And the tidy textbook rationale — that parallel spins keep electrons apart and lower their mutual repulsion — misstates the mechanism, which is dominated instead by increased attraction to the nucleus.
misreadings: It is not a single rule but three, of which chemistry courses usually teach only the first. And the reason maximum spin wins is not, as commonly taught, that spread-out electrons repel one another less — accurate calculations show the repulsion can even be greater, and the real driver is stronger electron-nucleus attraction from reduced screening.
origin: Formulated by the German physicist Friedrich Hund from spectroscopic data in 1925 and set out in his 1927 monograph on line spectra and the periodic system; the three rules for the ground-state term follow from the Russell-Saunders coupling scheme.
